name: Sam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and run an excavator at a large iron-ore mine, usually cleaning the face before the haul trucks come through. I've got a two-year technical diploma and lead a small crew because I can judge a bucketful without throwing half of it over the side. The pay is low for this job, and rent plus helping replace my partner's broken glasses has left less than a month's expenses saved. I like a clean, well-kept machine; I don't use AI and I hate being handed a new screen halfway through a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'd rather have fresh hydraulic hoses than another promise about clever software changing the whole mine. I don't mind the office saving time, provided somebody still answers the parts phone when my excavator stops working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the excavator work to continue, but rent day still has me checking which bills can wait until payday. A skilled operator on low pay can still be one bad week away from asking a relative for petrol money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the excavator and keep the handwritten inspection sheet beside the cab door on every shift. I'd stop buying canteen lunches from Monday and take leftovers until the next two rent payments are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious already, before anybody says AI. Last week I kept the cab heater low because I was thinking about the electricity bill waiting at home, which makes no sense but that's where my head went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would wait first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone can be a few days late before the rent can. My partner needs the phone too, so even that isn't a simple little saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small software change be a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if somebody shows me exactly what I need to do and leaves the old instructions nearby. I won't start typing guesses into something I don't understand while a truck is waiting for a load.

say: I'd tell the crew I'd rather have **fresh hydraulic hoses** than another promise about clever software changing the whole mine.
I don't mind the office saving time, provided somebody still answers the **parts phone** when my excavator stops working.
think: I expect the excavator work to continue, but **rent day** still has me checking which bills can wait until payday.
A skilled operator on **low pay** can still be one bad week away from asking a relative for petrol money.
do: Keep operating the **excavator** and keep the handwritten inspection sheet beside the cab door on every shift.
Stop buying **canteen lunches** from Monday and take leftovers until the next two rent payments are covered.
feel: **Anxious about money**, even though no major change threatens the excavator role.
S0.quote: A skilled operator on low pay can still be one bad week away from asking a relative for petrol money.
fieldNote: His **baseline worry** concerns low earnings and short reserves, while the physical excavator role appears stable under modest routine automation.
Preference for **familiar methods** shapes an unchanged paper inspection routine; his immediate financial response is a specific reduction in purchased meals.

steps.text: Operate the excavator and keep the handwritten inspection routine
Take leftover lunches until the next two rent payments are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch is changing, not that somebody has invented a machine that can load every awkward corner overnight. Before a new system reaches the cab, I want a named trainer beside me rather than a password in an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work looks safe for now, but I'd struggle if new targets reduced breaks or turned mistakes into lost shifts. The empty rent buffer still worries me more than office software; I can't pay a bill with an optimistic announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to demonstrate the new dispatch instructions in person before changing the route I follow between loading areas. I'd keep taking packed lunches and record the savings until I can cover an unexpected week's loss of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the same bills and irritated by having to admit I need somebody beside me. I still expect to drive the excavator, but a confusing instruction feels more serious when I can't afford to lose a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you refuse the new instructions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to guess if I thought the route wasn't safe. Show me on the ground and let me repeat the instruction back, and I can follow a proper procedure without becoming a fan of the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the supervisor about targets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a delay while learning counts against us and get the answer before the change. I'm not trying to turn it into a political row; I just want to know the rules before somebody measures me against them.

say: I'd say **dispatch is changing**, not that somebody has invented a machine that can load every awkward corner overnight.
Before a new system reaches the cab, I want a **named trainer** beside me rather than a password in an email.
think: My hands-on work looks safe for now, but I'd struggle if **new targets** reduced breaks or turned mistakes into lost shifts.
The empty **rent buffer** still worries me more than office software; I can't pay a bill with an optimistic announcement.
do: Ask my **supervisor** to demonstrate the new dispatch instructions in person before changing the route I follow between loading areas.
Keep taking **packed lunches** and record the savings until I can cover an unexpected week's loss of wages.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, with added discomfort about unfamiliar instructions rather than expected immediate replacement.
S1.quote: The empty rent buffer still worries me more than office software; I can't pay a bill with an optimistic announcement.
fieldNote: His **resistance** concerns learning risk and accountability, not a claim that physical loading disappears as soon as thinking tasks change.
Continuing **household vulnerability** supports anxiety across both mild scenarios; he seeks a practical demonstration and retains the same affordable spending reduction.

steps.text: Request an in-person dispatch demonstration before changing the loading route
Keep taking packed lunches and track the money retained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 isn't the same as a robot excavator, but neither date gives me much comfort. If robots reach the mine around 2031, the managers need to say what happens to people who only know this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the mine to need fewer operators, and I've no useful plan beyond hoping my name stays on the rota. Two years feels like no time when I have no course chosen, no spare money and almost no other mines nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the home internet package to the cheapest basic option now and keep the difference for rent after 2028. I'd ask my older brother whether his spare room would be available if my mine wage disappears; make no booking yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm panicked, to be honest, and I keep going round the same numbers without finding an answer. Cutting a bill and asking about a room are things I can say out loud; neither tells me how I'd earn when the excavator doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen in the first year after 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving while the shifts existed and ring my brother when the worry got too much. The three extra years before robots don't calm me, because I can't picture what to do with the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops you choosing a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every advert seems to say the same thing about a bright future, and I don't know anyone who got a job from one. I'd be terrified of spending rent money and discovering I'd only bought a folder and a certificate.

say: I'd say **thinking AI in 2028** isn't the same as a robot excavator, but neither date gives me much comfort.
If robots reach the mine around **2031**, the managers need to say what happens to people who only know this work.
think: I expect the mine to need **fewer operators**, and I've no useful plan beyond hoping my name stays on the rota.
Two years feels like **no time** when I have no course chosen, no spare money and almost no other mines nearby.
do: Cut the **home internet package** to the cheapest basic option now and keep the difference for rent after 2028.
Ask my **older brother** whether his spare room would be available if my mine wage disappears; make no booking yet.
feel: **Panicked and stuck**, with no workable employment plan or reserve despite trying emergency household measures.
S2.quote: I expect the mine to need fewer operators, and I've no useful plan beyond hoping my name stays on the rota.
fieldNote: He describes **overwhelm** without a credible income plan; emergency cuts and a possible family room offer little sense of control.
The **physical delay** is understood but not converted into preparation, consistent with unfamiliarity, limited local work and strong reluctance to risk money.

steps.text: Reduce the home internet package and keep the difference for rent
Ask an older brother about a spare room if wages disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should at least let the mine show us a proper working placement before planning changes in 2031. Don't tell me to buy a certificate now and hope somebody wants it when robot excavators come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect lost operator jobs, but I could visit a real workshop before deciding whether a different job is possible. The extra years help me ask questions; the thin savings mean I still can't gamble a month's rent on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd visit the mine maintenance workshop with my supervisor this year and ask whether any paid beginner placements actually exist. I'd keep a paper rent ledger and set aside ten each payday, carrying the habit into the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because I still think people doing my job will be cut. Five years lets me ask to see a workshop on a normal day, rather than feeling I have to sign a course form tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is visiting a workshop the same as deciding to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I'd want that understood before I walked in. I'd be asking what the jobs pay and watching somebody do the work, not agreeing to borrow money for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check after planning AI arrived in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at whether the mine had kept the placements open and whether trainees were actually being paid. Robots coming around 2034 still leaves a deadline, so I'd need evidence rather than another invitation to wait.

say: I'd say **five years** should at least let the mine show us a proper working placement before planning changes in 2031.
Don't tell me to buy a certificate now and hope somebody wants it when **robot excavators** come around 2034.
think: I still expect **lost operator jobs**, but I could visit a real workshop before deciding whether a different job is possible.
The extra years help me ask questions; the **thin savings** mean I still can't gamble a month's rent on a promise.
do: Visit the **mine maintenance workshop** with my supervisor this year and ask whether any paid beginner placements actually exist.
Keep a **paper rent ledger** and set aside ten each payday, carrying the habit into the first year after 2031.
feel: **Anxious but less overwhelmed**, with one modest investigation he can undertake while keeping wages.
S3.quote: The extra years help me ask questions; the thin savings mean I still can't gamble a month's rent on a promise.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** enables low-risk investigation without turning a resistant worker into a keen adopter or inventing a guaranteed maintenance vacancy.
His **baseline anxiety** and expected displacement persist, but the specific workplace visit offers more control than he feels under short warning.

steps.text: Visit the maintenance workshop and ask about real paid placements
Record expenses on paper and set aside ten each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years gives us time to check offers, not a reason to forget the change until 2036. I'd listen to a former operator earning a proper wage elsewhere more closely than to somebody selling a training package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 in 2036, with most of a working life left when robots could reach loading around 2039. I could learn something slowly if I saw it work, but the rent worries still start now rather than in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to arrange a conversation with a former excavator operator who found other paid work, without buying training yet. I'd repeat a yearly job check through 2037, comparing real openings and wages before deciding whether to leave the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the next bill, and I don't want a distant date used to brush that aside. The machine threat feels less like an order to jump tonight, though I still hate the thought of starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask that former operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how long the first wage took to arrive and whether the new job actually paid enough for rent. I'd also ask what went wrong, because a story without any difficult bits would make me suspicious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2037 if the openings look poor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the mine wage while it existed and ask for another look at paid placements before robots arrived around 2039. I wouldn't call doing nothing a plan, but I also wouldn't hand in my notice because a brochure told me to be brave.

say: I'd tell the crew **ten years** gives us time to check offers, not a reason to forget the change until 2036.
I'd listen to a **former operator** earning a proper wage elsewhere more closely than to somebody selling a training package.
think: I'll be **37 in 2036**, with most of a working life left when robots could reach loading around 2039.
I could learn something slowly if I saw it work, but the **rent worries** still start now rather than in ten years.
do: Ask my **supervisor** to arrange a conversation with a former excavator operator who found other paid work, without buying training yet.
Repeat a **yearly job check** through 2037, comparing real openings and wages before deciding whether to leave the mine.
feel: **Anxious about present money**, with a more distant work threat that feels possible to investigate carefully.
S4.quote: I'd listen to a former operator earning a proper wage elsewhere more closely than to somebody selling a training package.
fieldNote: His **remaining career** rules out retirement as an escape, while gradual evidence gathering fits his reluctance to make risky changes.
The plan remains **conditional**, involving actual workers and wages rather than assuming either a new occupation or a future local labour shortage.

steps.text: Discuss actual wages and transition costs with a former excavator operator
Keep mine shifts while reviewing real job openings each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 scares me most because planning changes could start soon and robot excavators around 2031 could take the thing I'm best at. I'd need somebody to show me a real paid job before asking me to give up this one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how you're meant to tell a useful course from somebody selling hope. I can judge a heavy bucket by feel; I can't judge whether a training advert is telling the truth.

headlineQuote: I can judge a heavy bucket by feel; I can't judge whether a training advert is telling the truth.
portrait: A **27-year-old excavator operator**, he leads a small mine crew and values the judgement that keeps each bucket safe and tidy.
His **technical diploma** and strong practical skill coexist with low pay, expensive rent and less than a month of expenses saved.
He avoids **unfamiliar technology**, distrusts training adverts and asks for direct evidence of real work before considering a change in occupation.
Short warning brings **panic** without an affordable employment plan; longer warnings allow cautious investigation while present financial worries persist.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves him expecting eventual excavator-job losses without money or a credible personal route into different work.
whatWouldHelp: A **real paid placement**, demonstrated by someone he trusts, would make investigating different work less frightening than buying an untested course.
